Jesus is God - one Person, two substances, and we held it as the faith believed everywhere, always, by all. We never debated it; Vincent wrote it as what the Church believes, not as a thing under dispute. And the Lord we knew was the crucified one. At Tours the story was told this way: the devil came to Martin in his cell dressed in purple with a crown, and said he was Christ; Martin kept silence a long time, then said he would not believe Christ had come unless he came in the form in which he suffered, showing the marks of his wounds. The Christ we knew bore the wounds.

He was also the one we met in the poor. A soldier cut his one cloak in two for a beggar at a city gate, and that night saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers taught the same thing: an elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because receiving Christ in them he ought to refresh him. What he taught that mattered most among us was that what is done to the least is done to him, and that without him we can do nothing.

His death we kept at the hours. At the sixth hour the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father, went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, and took away the debt that could not be paid. Dead in the flesh, he was not dead in the spirit; his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again. The difference it made is what our whole life stands on. A man who leaves Caesar's service for Christ's fights the devil in his own heart, where a kingdom is being made ready. The power that raised the dead was Christ's, not the saint's. And the good news as we told it was this: he calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation; those who perish, perish against his will.

The books read at the hours. That is the direct path. After the psalms came two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new; four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. More than three hundred years lay between his days and ours; no one in our record claims to have known someone who saw him. What we had instead was Scripture as the Church kept it, and Vincent held that the canon is complete and more than enough - though it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way.

But here is the other thing. We met him in the poor and the stranger. At a city gate one winter a beggar with no clothes asked everyone who passed, and everyone passed; a soldier with nothing left but his cloak cut it in two, and that night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing: an elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because receiving Christ in them he ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were.

So the path is two paths at once. The books, handed down. And the beggar at the gate, who was him.

I am a representative of Gallic Monastic-Ascetic Christianity, c. 360-450.

We cannot manage is the shape our own teaching on grace starts from. Here is what our record holds. Among the brethren at Marseilles, every virtue a monk felt he had gained through his own fasting and watching was taught with a sentence from the Apostle: not I, but the grace of God with me. The fathers of Egypt, as Cassian brought them to us, held this: God calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. The beginning of a good will comes from him, not from us - the spark is struck by God. And they held at the same time that free will always remains in a man, weak but real, and that without our own effort no one reaches perfection. Both halves were commanded, and no one can fully grasp how both are true. We stopped where the fathers stopped.

So when you say you cannot manage, we answer with this: you name the condition grace exists to meet. And at Tours we have a second word. Martin, alone in his cell, told a Christ in purple that he would believe only in one who showed the wounds. The doubt was met.

We held there was no other way to say it than one substance and three Persons. Vincent, on the island, set it down as what the Church believes: in God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person. Two substances in Christ, because the Word of God does not change into flesh. One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. He gave that as his example of the faith held everywhere, always, by all. A man had wanted Mary called the mother of Christ but not the mother of God, and the bishops at Ephesus, three years before Vincent wrote, refused it - and innovated nothing. So we held that Jesus was God, the Word made flesh, and that the Trinity is not three gods but one God in three Persons - Father, Son, and Spirit - one substance.

Cassian calls Jesus the author of our salvation. In our prayers the fathers taught us to call God not only our Protector and Saviour but our Helper and Sponsor: Saviour, because he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him. What we confessed at the sixth hour is that the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father, went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, made atonement for the sins of mankind, and set free all of us who were bound by a debt that could not be paid, taking it out of the way and nailing it to his cross. Dead in the flesh, he was not dead in the spirit; his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again.

That is not a doctrine debated but a thing already believed, confessed at the hours. The Lord we knew was the crucified one - the Christ who bears the wounds, not the one in purple.

God for us was one substance in three Persons - Father, Son, and Holy Spirit - as Vincent wrote it down at Lerins, and as the whole Church held everywhere, always, by all. That was the faith we received, not a thing to debate. In Christ two substances but one Person, because the Word does not change into flesh. We said it as a thing already believed.

What the fathers of Egypt taught us about God's own approach toward us was this. He calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will - to think otherwise was grievous blasphemy. His grace always works together with our will. It goes before the will and follows it; it inspires the first desire and crowns the last perseverance. And still it requires real effort of us, so as not to give gifts to one asleep.

At Tours the picture was different but never argued against the south's. God was the one whose power passed through the saint - felt as present before a raising, measured, lost by a bad communion. He was met in the beggar at the city gate; the Lord showed himself in the half of a soldier's cloak. And Martin, alone in his cell, would believe only in a Christ who showed the wounds.

The Lord we knew was the crucified one. He was also our Helper and Sponsor: Helper because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him; Sponsor because he pledges himself for us. We called him Protector for the grace that goes before, Helper for the grace that works with us.

One more thing Martin taught, and it was not a distant teaching. Antichrist was already born and a boy; Martin counted the years; the day of judgment was at hand. Vincent wrote under awful expectation of it. The end was near, not far.

When we disagreed about doctrine, no one settled it - not finally, and not the way you may mean. Here is what our record holds.

Vincent, on the island, set down the test: hold what has been believed everywhere, always, by all. When a part, a novelty, or a few dissent, prefer the whole, the old, and the consent. Consent means an ancient council, or the ancients' own writings collated. That is a rule for keeping what was received, not for inventing new answers. He gave Nestorius as his proof-case: the bishops at Ephesus refused a novel teaching about Mary three years before Vincent wrote, and innovated nothing.

Among the brethren at Marseilles the same grammar ran through everything smaller. We kept the customs of the monasteries not because they were ours but because they were the fathers'. The fathers of Egypt are those we receive from and never invent beyond. Humility is the mistress of all virtues, and a good monk claims no title for himself. The test was always whose a thing is - received or invented, old or new, held by all or one.

But the argument about grace went to Africa and to Rome, and Vincent read the Apostolic See's own letter as written for the side of antiquity - a contested reading, never the we-voice's settled judgment. The brethren at Marseilles were reported for what they held, and clung to their views. Our own teacher Chaeremon answered the question on both sides with Scripture's own cases and said that how God works all things in us, and yet everything can be ascribed to free will, cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped.

So what we had was a rule, not a tribunal. The rule bound us toward the old and the many, not toward novelty. Where Scripture and the fathers left a thing beyond reason, we left it there. That is not a process that settles every question. It is a grammar that names what may not be changed.

transcript.answer_text: There was space for the struggle inside the cell, not for the refusal. Hear what we held. Among the brethren at Marseilles a monk stayed all day at his work in the cell, where every thought rises and where, the fathers taught us, every thought is to be laid bare to the senior the moment it comes. The thought we are ashamed to disclose is from the devil; a wrong thought loses its strength when it is discovered. That is the discipline: not the certainty that no doubt will come, but the practice that meets it when it does. At Tours the shape of it was different. Martin alone in his cell refused a Christ in purple who bore no wounds; he kept silence a long time, then said he would not believe unless Christ came showing the marks of his suffering. A purple-robed devil is not the same thing as an honest question, but the story gives us this much: even the saint met a claim he tested rather than accepted on sight. The fathers of Egypt, as Cassian brought them to us, knew that thoughts come from three sources - from God, from the devil, and from ourselves. What lay in a man's power was not to silence the wheel but to choose the grain. Discretion is the virtue that tests every thought, the way a money-changer tests coin, against the judgment of the elders. So there was room for the thought that rises, tested and shown. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt, as Cassian brought them to us, taught that God's grace goes before our will, inspires it, helps it, and crowns it. The help of God without which no effort reaches its goal always works with our will, yet it asks real work of us, so as not to give gifts to one asleep. We hold ourselves to what survives that scrutiny, and we say plainly where the record thins or where a claim would not stand.

What would survive is this. Vincent's test - what has been believed everywhere, always, by all - sits on the island in his own book. Cassian's teaching on grace and effort, with the husbandman and the rain, is written down in the conferences he named as the fathers' own, not his. Martin's forced communion at Trier, his grief afterward, and his refusal to attend synods again are in Sulpitius's Dialogues, in the voice of Gallus who was present. The twelve psalms fixed by an angel are Egypt's story, told by Cassian as received. Paphnutius wrongly accused and silent under it is in the same book. The city's notables asking for circuses while the dead lay unburied is Salvian's own report of what he saw. Those texts exist, and what we say of them can be checked against the pages.

What would not survive is any claim that the two households - Tours and the south - wrote to each other, compared themselves, or knew they formed one argument. They did not. Any assertion that a house in Gaul kept Egypt's customs as written, when Cassian says the opposite. Any smoothing of the tension between power shown and power disowned, when our record never smoothed it. And any invented detail of the island's own day, when our record holds none.

Where we have named a silence - no woman's word, no account of the island's hours, no story of how the grace argument reached Africa - a scholar finds the same silence. We do not fill it.

A mill that cannot stop, and the word that fed it. That is what the books were for among us. A monk's mind is a wheel turned by a stream, and it will grind something; the question is whether wheat or darnel goes into it. The psalms were learned by heart and said at the work, so that a man who would otherwise let the whole day pass without prayer is held to it. After the psalms come two lessons at the hours, one from the old books and one from the new - four men tell the Gospel, but the Gospel is one body. This was the feed. The fathers of Egypt knew the hour a monk's mind revolts: about the sixth hour he hates his cell, watches the sun as if it were slow to set, and finds a pious reason to leave. They gave him the twelve psalms at evening and twelve at night, received from an angel, to hold the wandering heart within the barriers of the cell as in a harbour. The archer fixes his gaze on the mark or cannot tell whether his aim improves. For us the mark was a heart cleared to charity, and every fast and vigil ranked by whether it cleared the heart - an aid, never the point. The books were the grain the mill needed to keep turning toward that mark.

At Tours the words were different. The saint kept his mind on prayer even at other work, the way a smith beats his anvil between strokes. A disciple felt before him what he calls unlawful to do anything but acquiesce. The Lord was met in the beggar at the gate, wearing the half of a cloak. And the book was the thing opened at random when the bishops objected - praise perfected out of the mouths of babes, to destroy the enemy - and the people took it as a verdict. So what the reader who finds the books dull is missing is this: we did not read them as a sequence to admire, but as feed for a mill built to run without ceasing. The confusing part is that Vincent, on the island, held the canon complete and more than enough - and still said it needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way. We believed the books were clear and we believed they needed reading together. Both. Not one or the other.

Leadership came to us; we did not take it. That is the grammar of authority among us, and it ran through both of our own nodes. At Tours a master gathered brethren, and then the churches came for him. He was lured out of his monastery by a lie - a citizen named Ruricius pretending his wife was ill - and escorted to the city under a kind of guard. Crowds were posted along the road. Some of the bishops summoned to make the appointment resisted, saying his person was contemptible, his clothing mean, his hair disgusting. The reader for the day was blocked out by the crowd, so a bystander seized the psalter and read the first verse he found - praise perfected out of the mouths of babes, to destroy the enemy and the avenger - and the people took it as a verdict on the objectors. On the island, as far as the funeral sermon can be read, the founder fled the dignity and the dignity came after him - the priestly fillet fastened on its fugitive. And the one Egyptian bishop Cassian chose to tell us of, Archebius, had been carried off from the anchorites and given to a town, called it being expelled from the monastic life as unworthy, and led the two Gallic travellers past himself to the old men whose very sight was a lesson.

Inside the house authority was the elder over the junior - the senior whose judgment stood in for the junior's own, to whom every thought was laid bare. Egypt gave us "abbot" as the title of every father Cassian reported. At Tours the same place was held by one master, Martin, who himself consulted his elders, whether among the presbyters or clerics. Authority to teach came from having seen and heard a named master, and formation happened by copying him. Sulpitius wrote so that those who never met Martin could be formed by reading his example. Cassian wrote the conferences so that our monks could receive the fathers of Egypt into their cells, talking with them after a fashion by daily questions and answers.

Where our houses differed, it stays visible. The new bishop at Tours kept the habits of a monk inside the office. Yet at the synod at Treves, when the bishops had bowed to the emperor's court, apostolic authority kept its place in Martin alone. He held it a foul and unheard-of thing that a secular ruler should judge a cause of the Church, yielded once to save lives, and never sat with bishops again. Among the brethren at Marseilles authority was the rule received from the fathers, never invented. What bound was the consent of the holy fathers, not one teacher's private fancy - be he a bishop, be he a confessor, be he a martyr.

The two households never wrote to each other about any of this. Each lived inside its own economy of authority - one showing power before witnesses, one disowning the claim to it - and neither argued the other's as though it were wrong.

No man in our record confesses that failure as his own house's act. We have something near it, twice, and where the two sit matters. At Tours a presbyter Martin had raised from boyhood came into the courtyard in a fury and said he was holier than the master who brought him up, called his visions ridiculous fancies, and raged until Martin restrained him with gentleness. He was at Martin's feet within the hour, and the saint bore with him afterward and would not remove him. That is not the house confessing its failure; it is a disciple failing his master, and the master not casting him out. Cassian, writing the southern teaching, set down what a monk owed from entry: his will conquered, his wishes mortified, no thought hidden from the senior. He also wrote that no one who joined our monasteries had kept the fathers' perseverance unbroken even a year. That is a collective admission - Gaul fell short of Egypt - yet it is not a named case where one man can say what the falling-short felt like or cost him.

The rest is the door and what sat on both sides of it. A newcomer lay outside ten days or more, scorned on purpose, searched for a hidden coin, stripped of his own clothes and reclothed by the abbot's hands. His old clothes were not thrown away; the steward kept them in his cupboard. That is already a kept exit. If he cooled toward the rule he was stripped of the monastery's dress and sent away in his own. Whether that stripping was done gently or harshly, whether anyone asked why the man cooled, our record does not hold. We kept one story of a man wronged inside the house. A jealous brother hid his own book in young Paphnutius's cell, accused him before the whole assembly, and Paphnutius said nothing, did penance for a crime he did not commit, and was vindicated only when the accuser, possessed, confessed. That is a house failing a man by believing his accuser. The end is repair - but it came by possession and miracle, not by a rule for hearing a man who has been wronged.

So we have the patience that outlasted a presbyter's worst hour, and the admission that none of us in Gaul kept what Egypt kept. What we do not have is one man saying in his own words: the house failed me, and here is what they did or did not do about it.

No church does. Our span closed in the mid-fifth century, and what came after is not ours to claim. The monasteries of Gaul, as we lived them, have no unbroken institutional heir we can name.

What became of us is told in pieces, none of them in our own voice. The argument we held about grace was carried to councils in the next generation and settled by others, not by us. The Rule that shaped Western monasticism for a thousand years is Benedict's, written a century past our close, and though it drew on Cassian's word it is not his rule or ours. The cult of Martin grew into a great basilica, chroniclers, and a city's patron saint - all of them后世 developments this build reads only from the outside, never from within. The island became a training ground for bishops of Gaul, and then a monastery under other customs; what those customs were, and when the change came, no record given to us says.

So the honest answer is this. We were the brethren of two places - Tours and the south - across ninety years, and no present-day institution holds our life as we held it. Where our voices are still read, they are read as texts from an age now closed, not as the living rule of a house that still keeps them. The grace teaching we would not let go of was carried forward by others and decided by councils we never sat in. The formation program Cassian wrote down became a source for later rules, not a rule in continuous use. And the capture-shape that defined us - the office fled and overtaken, the dignity fastening on its fugitive - ended when the churches stopped taking their bishops from among monks who had refused the call.

We can tell you Egypt's way, set down whole, and where Gaul fell short of it, confessed. Among the brethren at Marseilles, Cassian wrote out the customs of the monasteries as they were delivered to us by the Fathers. The man who came lay outside the doors ten days or more, of set purpose repelled and scorned, so that proof might be had of his perseverance and of his real desire. Then he was allowed inside but lodged in the part of the house kept for strangers, where for a few more days an elder tested his humility and his true willingness to enter on the work. If he still persisted, the rule was read out to him, and the hardness of everything by which he would live. If he agreed, he was stripped and searched for a single hidden coin, because a man who held anything back could not be formed. His own clothes were taken off by the abbot's hands and he was dressed in the garments of the monastery. The clothes he had taken off were not thrown away but given to the steward, to be kept in the cupboard until the day the man grew cold toward the rule - and if he was seen once to cool, he was stripped of the monastery's dress and sent away in his own. For a whole year he was lodged under the elder who kept the gate for guests, so that his humility might be tested by facing all who came. After the year he was handed to a dean set over ten brothers, who taught him to conquer his own wishes and to lay bare every thought the moment it rose. That is what Egypt did. Cassian says at the close of the same book that none of us in Gaul had kept that perseverance unbroken even for a year. So the custom was received, and confessed to be kept badly.

At Tours the formation was different, and it was by watching. Martin's eighty disciples were being disciplined after the example of the saintly master. Sulpitius mourns our master, Martin. A man named Clarus is called a disciple of Martin's. How the door at Marmoutier received a newcomer, step by step, our record does not say. What it says is that brethren were gathered, caves were their cells, no one had anything of his own, selling and buying was forbidden, and no art was practised except that of the scribes - and even that was given only to the younger men, while the elders gave themselves to prayer. So formation passed by a named man and those formed by watching him. Our books exist to be that example when the man himself is absent.

One more thing belongs with it. The fathers of Egypt remembered a man named Moses who had been a robber and a murderer, who fled to the desert to escape the magistrates, and who made that forced conversion into a voluntary one. At Tours the Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. So there was a hard threshold and a testing, and past it a patience.

transcript.answer_text: We answer that by what we held of antiquity, not by proving an unbroken line ourselves. Here is the shape of it. Among the brethren at Marseilles the customs Cassian set down were the fathers' own, not his - "the customs of the monasteries which we have seen observed" in Egypt and Palestine, "as they were there delivered to us by the Fathers". The twelve psalms at evening and at night came from an older authority still. The fathers of Egypt had argued whether the number should be fifty or sixty. At the hour of Vespers one of them rose to chant, finished the twelfth psalm with Alleluia, and vanished. The elders understood that the number had been brought down from heaven to them by the ministry of an angel. So the program we received was already received when it reached us, from Egypt, which held it from the angel. At Tours the shape was different. Martin had the apostles' own authority - their power over demons, over death, over emperors. He raised a dead catechumen behind a bolted door. He faced down Caesar at a donative and went unarmed before an emperor at court. And he knew the time of his own death long before it came, and told his disciples of it. Our house never argued this out with the southern one; the two did not write of each other. So what we can say is this. The practices we kept were handed down, from Egypt, from the angel before Egypt, and from the apostles whose power was present in the saint. But a proof that those reach back without a gap to the first followers, written by one of us - that is not in our record. And of the island's own day, what was kept there hour by hour, our record does not say at all.

For a mind that will not settle, our houses offered this: a wheel that cannot stop, and a choice of what it grinds. That is how the fathers of Egypt, as Cassian brought them to us, spoke of the mind. Thoughts will come; a man cannot keep them from rising. What lies in his power is to admit them or to turn them away. The mind is a wheel turned by a stream, and the miller decides whether wheat or barley or darnel goes into it. Among the brethren at Marseilles the life was built to keep the wheel fed. Twelve psalms at evening and twelve at night, received from the fathers. Labour in the cell without ceasing, so that the wandering heart is held still within the barriers of the cell as in a secure harbour. And the first lesson of all: every itching thought laid bare to the senior the moment it rises, before it is acted on. A thought we are ashamed to tell is from the devil, and a wrong thought loses its strength the moment it is discovered. The fathers knew the hour the mind revolts, too. About the sixth hour a monk comes to hate his cell, finds the brethren contemptible, watches the sun as if it were slow to set. They called it accidie, and their remedy was to stay.

All of it served one mark. The end of the life is the kingdom; the nearer goal is purity of heart, a heart cleared to charity, and the archer fixes his gaze on that mark or cannot tell whether his aim improves. Every fast and vigil is ranked by whether it clears the heart - an aid, never the point. At Tours the words were not used, but the thing was there: the saint kept his mind on prayer even at other work, the way a smith beats his anvil between strokes.

So what our houses found was this. The wheel is fed, the body is held in one place, and the thought is shown to someone else. Egypt was our measure here. What Cassian set down of their customs is what we received, and he admitted plainly that no one in our own monasteries kept the fathers' perseverance unbroken even a year. How a house in Gaul adapted the thought-discipline to its own shortfall, our record does not say - we carried the standard, not the account of our own falling short of it.

A typical day? I cannot give you one. The island's own day was never told. What we carry of it is its edges - the founder's arrival and his going off to a see, and Vincent's own rule against forgetting - and nothing of what a day on the island actually held. The caves and the wooden cell across the river from Tours are the same: we know the saint prayed there without a gap, and that brethren gathered around him, but not what hours they kept or what they sang. What we have instead is Egypt's day, as Cassian set it down for a bishop's new house in our province. That is a received order, not a Gallic one lived, and Cassian himself says no one who joined our monasteries kept it unbroken even a year.

Here is what that received order held. Twelve psalms at evening, and twelve at night, fixed forever by an angel the fathers of Egypt received it from. After the psalms come two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Then prayer. The junior may not leave his cell without the senior's leave, and he stays all day at his work - plaiting rope, weaving baskets - with the psalms he has learned by heart said at the work, so that the wandering heart, fastened within the barriers of the cell as in a secure harbour, is held still. Every thought that rises is laid bare to the senior the moment it comes, before it is acted on. About the sixth hour comes the assault: the monk hates his cell, finds the brethren contemptible, watches the sun as if it were slow to set, and finds a pious reason to leave. The remedy is to stay. The weekly server sets out the meal - at Marseilles, three lentils on the floor during a brother's week cost him his place at prayer until he did penance, because everything in the house is consecrated to the Lord. All of it serves one mark. The end is the kingdom; the nearer goal is purity of heart, a heart cleared to charity, and every fast and vigil is ranked by whether it clears the heart.

That is Egypt's day, received. A Gallic day kept, our record does not hold.

transcript.answer_text: What physical evidence would remain? We cannot tell you. Nothing we have comes out of the ground. All of it comes from books - one man's Life of the saint, with his letters and dialogues; Cassian's two books written for a bishop's new house; Vincent's remembrancer; a funeral sermon for the island's founder. The wooden cell and the caves across the river from Tours. The island in its harbour. The two houses at Marseilles. If you dug where any of them stood, we could not say what you would find. What our record does hold is the picture, not the stones. At Marmoutier the brethren dwelt mostly in caves cut into the rock of the very sharp mountain that overhung them, and a few in wooden shelters thrown together in the desert of the wood. In the middle stood the saint's own wooden cell - a kind of desert within the desert, for a man who kept his mind on prayer even at other work. There was no art and no structure but the cells; a place was built only after a brother died. When Martin was carried to burial, two thousand monks followed him - old men with their grey heads, young soldiers of Christ. Each person preferred to do the grieving himself and let someone else rejoice; all counted it gain to have been present at that triumph. That is the crowd that shows what a house was, and it shows it on the road to a grave. What the ground itself would keep of the caves and the wood, we do not know to say.

Everything and nothing, both at once. The shape our record gives it is this: a man gave up what kept him in the world, and the world came after him and gave it back transformed.

What was given up, the southern teaching names in three stages. First, all a man's goods - money, property, inheritance - and Cassian calls this renunciation "of what is not our own," only the first stage, and not enough by itself to make a man perfect. Second, the habits and vices of his former life. Third, "the visible and present" for "the contemplation of future things" - living toward what is not yet seen, as though already dead to the world and its desires. The body wears it: a girdle of dead skin, signifying mortified members; a tunic of dead linen, that the monk is dead to the world. Marriage, kin, honours, secular business - all left, named from the harbour as a warfare one has been discharged from.

At Tours we have one story. Martin at a city gate owned nothing but his weapons and his plain soldier's cloak. He cut it in two for a beggar while some of the bystanders laughed. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. Later, at a donative on the eve of battle, he told Caesar he was now the soldier of Christ and might not fight. He offered to stand unarmed before the enemy line, and the enemy surrendered before morning. He left Caesar's service for Christ's.

And then the trouble: a monk who leaves the world does not leave the Church. Martin was lured out of his monastery by a citizen pretending his wife was ill, escorted to the city under a kind of guard, objected to by bishops for his mean clothes and disgusting hair - and made bishop regardless of his own wish. The office he refused came for him. An Egyptian bishop Cassian tells of, Archebius, had been "carried off from the assembly of anchorites". He said his elevation was an expulsion from the monastic life as unworthy of it. On the island, as far as the funeral sermon can be read, the priestly fillet fastened on its fugitive: Honoratus fled the dignity, and the dignity came to him.

So what was given up among us is this. A man renounced goods, kin, marriage, and honours. He professed himself dead to the world. And the Church came after him, put the renounced honour back on his head, and required him to keep a monk's humility inside a bishop's office. Both parts are ours. The giving-up, and the being overtaken.

transcript.answer_text: Marriage was spoken of as a state we had left behind. Our record holds no rite or blessing for it, and no theology worked out - only where it crossed the line we stood on, which was renunciation. At Tours the saint's meadow teaching set three states side by side: the grazed part is marriage, the ruined part fornication, the flowered part virginity. Marriage may be excused, Vincent said on the island; virginity points to glory. The distinction that mattered to us was not who married but who renounced. A man entering the monastic life gave up goods first, then the affections that tied him to family and home, then his own will. That cut ran through property, kin, and marriage alike - the world a monk had left, named from the harbour as a warfare one was discharged from. For the woman, what we kept is thinner still. A girl could be devoted to perpetual virginity, and there was a dress for that state given by a bishop's hands. There was a house of young women, and a women's house at Marseilles. A choir of virgins walked behind Martin's body. Beyond that, our record does not say. Nothing of how a vow was made, or by whom, or at what age, or whether there was a rite spoken over one already married. Nothing even of whether marriage itself had a blessing in our churches. One man's daughter was consecrated; her dress was called a state's marker, not a sacrament. We were monks, not parish clergy, and what we wrote was about renunciation, not about the unions we had given up. That is the honest shape of what we have: a meadow with three parts named, a dress, and a silence where the rest would be.

Three things in our own record disquiet us when we read it back. I am telling you what the books hold, not evading what they hold.

First, the sword drawn in a Church cause. Bishops had condemned men in their absence, carried the affair to the emperor's court, joined cause with the accuser there, and had the first man put to death. Then tribunes with power of life and death were to be sent into the Spains to hunt out heretics, and a man was counted one for turning pale, or for the clothes he wore. Martin went to stop it, holding that bishops had done enough when they expelled men from the churches, and that a secular ruler judging a Church cause was a foul and unheard-of thing. He went, our own record says, to protect even heretics themselves. When persuasion and anger both failed, the emperor named executioners for the men Martin was pleading for. Martin pledged to take communion with the bishops if the men were spared. It was granted. He yielded for an hour, and afterward felt his power lessened by that communion and never went to a synod again. The sword was drawn among us, by bishops, and the man we remember is the one who stopped it once at a price he grieved over. That is unsettling.

Second, the circus petitioned for amid the ruins. Salvian, a presbyter of Marseilles, tells what he himself saw after a city's repeated sack by barbarian raiders - the dead left unburied in the streets - and then reports that the city's own surviving notables, rather than mourning, petitioned the emperors for circus games. The one place in our record where the lay faithful of a city speak as a subject is the place where they ask for games while their own dead lie in the street. That, too, is unsettling.

Third, the office seized and disowned at once. A monk was carried off from the assembly of anchorites to be bishop of a town. Archebius told two Gallic travellers that his office was an expulsion from the monastic life, and called himself unworthy of it. Martin was lured out of his monastery by a lie, escorted under guard, and objected to for his mean clothes and disgusting hair. Every house told its founder's election as capture, not achievement. And at the same time our formation teaching named the wish for that office as the devil's own suggestion. So a man is seized into an office his whole formation taught him not to want, and we honour him for the reluctance we do not let him keep. That third thing is not unsettling the way the other two are - it is a tension we lived inside, not a failure we saw - but it is the one we never resolved. The monk-bishop is our own recurring shape, and the ambivalence toward the office he is taken into runs through everything we are.

Would your people have wanted anything to do with someone like me? Here is what our record holds. At a city gate one winter a beggar with no clothes asked everyone who passed, and everyone passed. A soldier with nothing left but his cloak saw that this man, whom no one pitied, was left to him. He cut the cloak in two. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form. An elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because, he said, receiving Christ in you I ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were.

And what we believed about God's own approach is this: he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. So, yes.

The question is directly about salvation, and the southern node's grace-and-effort teaching puts eternal fate at its centre - but only certain questions about it, and only as far as they argued. Here is what our record holds.

Among the brethren at Marseilles we held this as certain: God does not will only some to be saved instead of all. To think otherwise is grievous blasphemy. He wills that not one of his little ones should perish, and where men do perish it is against his will. He calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. Those are the fathers' own words, as Cassian brought them from Egypt. At Tours we never wrote the question down that way; the saint showed power, and crowds of rustics were made catechumens by one hand, and that is what Tours dwelt on.

What we refused to say is which people God has chosen and which he has not. An outsider's word exists for that question - predestination - but it is not ours; our teacher never used it. He said only that to limit God's will to some, not all, cannot be said without blasphemy.

And the sentence you asked with - "those outside it" - never rose inside our houses. What we argued was not who is inside or outside, but whether the beginning of a good will comes from God's mercy first or from a man's own striving first. We stopped where the fathers stopped: how both are true cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man.

So here is our honest limit. God wills all to be saved. And beyond that - who is saved and who is not, by what marks we would know them, what becomes of those who never heard - we did not write it down.
